title: The five ways
hookLine: Aquinas offers five paths from the world to God, like motion needing a first mover
last: BY DOUBTING WE COME TO INQUIRY.

lines: COLD, BUT IT COULD BE HOT.
cards: A kettle sits on a stove. The water in it is cold, but it could be hot. Turn on the flame, and the heat that's really in the fire passes into the water, and the water starts to move.
Nothing mysterious about that. But a Dominican friar named Thomas Aquinas looked at moments exactly this ordinary, and asked where the chain of them leads.
His answer opens with a plain sentence: the existence of God can be proved in five ways. And the first way starts with something moving.

teach.b: For Aquinas, motion means any change at all: something that could be one way becoming that way. His own example is fire making wood hot. The wood can be hot; the fire actually is hot; so the fire moves the wood.
The rule he draws: whatever is moved is moved by another. The wood by the fire, the fire by something else, all at once, like a hand moving a stick that moves a stone.

That chain can't go on to infinity, he argues, or there would be no first mover, and so no other mover either. So there must be a first mover, moved by nothing, and this, he says, everyone understands to be God.
The other four ways follow the same shape. Causes, which need a first cause.

teach.h: THAT GOD IS, NOT WHAT GOD IS.
teach.b: Things that come and go, which need something that doesn't come and go. Things more or less good and true, which point to what is best and truest.
And things without minds that still act toward a goal, like an arrow flying straight because an archer aimed it. Two more details.
Aquinas starts from the world, not from an idea in the mind; he wasn't persuaded that God's existence is obvious to us just from the definition. And he never says the five ways tell us everything.
They show that God is, not what God is. Some truths about God, he says, reason can't reach without God revealing them.
Paul wrote that God's invisible things are "clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Aquinas took him at his word, and started with a moving world.

how: Catholic schools and seminaries teach Aquinas's five ways as part of philosophy, and Christians of other churches meet them in theology and apologetics classes, where they are still debated.

games.q: you're Aquinas. the wood is moved by the fire, the fire by something else, and on. what do you conclude?
o: there must be a first mover, moved by nothing.
nothing can be said about it.

practice: Find something moving: a curtain in a version, leaves outside, steam from a cup, your own chest rising. Watch it, then ask what moves it, and follow the chain back a few links, gently, without needing an answer.
If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you watched move.
